summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from highthroughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler
summary.executive_summary: The design of heterogeneous catalysts is hindered by the complexity of materials and the scarcity of high-performing candidates within the vast space of possible compositions. This study demonstrates the application of subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence to a hybrid dataset combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations to identify design rules for selective oxidation catalysts. The researchers synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. Using the yield of value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid) as the target, the SGD approach identified specific constraints on key physicochemical parameters that exclusively describe materials with outstanding performance. The identified rules constrain the reaction temperature to 280–300°C, the phosphorus content to >0.55, and the composition-weighted electronegativity to 3.910–4.002 eV. These rules not only rationalize the local reactivity patterns associated with exceptional performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts. By applying these rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts containing additional elements such as tellurium and tantalum. Experimental validation showed that these new materials achieved oxygenate yields up to 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively, which are significantly higher than the maximum yield of 26.85% observed in the three-component training set. The study highlights that while the temperature rule was not directly transferable to the more complex materials, the composition-dependent rules successfully predicted high-performing candidates, demonstrating the potential of SGD for rational catalyst design in complex materials spaces.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The design of heterogeneous catalysts is hindered by the complexity of materials and the scarcity of high-performing candidates within the vast space of possible compositions. This study demonstrates the application of subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence to a hybrid dataset combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations to identify design rules for selective oxidation catalysts. The researchers synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. Using the yield of value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid) as the target, the SGD approach identified specific constraints on key physicochemical parameters that exclusively describe materials with outstanding performance. The identified rules constrain the reaction temperature to 280–300°C, the phosphorus content to >0.55, and the composition-weighted electronegativity to 3.910–4.002 eV. These rules not only rationalize the local reactivity patterns associated with exceptional performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts. By applying these rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts containing additional elements such as tellurium and tantalum. Experimental validation showed that these new materials achieved oxygenate yields up to 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively, which are significantly higher than the maximum yield of 26.85% observed in the three-component training set. The study highlights that while the temperature rule was not directly transferable to the more complex materials, the composition-dependent rules successfully predicted high-performing candidates, demonstrating the potential of SGD for rational catalyst design in complex materials spaces.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis is governed by an intricate interplay of multiple processes. The explicit atomistic modelling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) is used to test large amounts of materials. Utilizing the information obtained by the experiments to decide on the next promising materials is not straightforward. The number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Detailed characterization of each material in large libraries is typically not feasible. Distinct catalytic mechanisms might operate depending on the materials and reaction conditions. Global models trained to describe all materials simultaneously may not allow focused modelling. Alternative approaches for catalyst design are therefore required.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints on their values. These rules are particularly associated with high performance in selective oxidation. The reactivity measured by HTE is used as the target in the SGD analysis. Temperature and composition-dependent physicochemical properties evaluated with DFT are used as candidate parameters. The hypothesis is that SGD can identify local behavior reflecting specific underlying processes. The approach circumvents the need for explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression. Candidate descriptive materials parameters can be calculated by first-principles methods. The resulting SG rules can identify promising catalyst candidates not yet synthesized. The goal is to describe materials and conditions giving high yields of oxygenates.

Methodological Details
120 different three-component catalyst compositions containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized. The catalysts were supported on SiO2 pseudo-liquid support. Reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors. The reaction feed included Ar, H2O, N2, O2, and propylene. Molar rates were 4.015, 4.015, 104.40, 20.08, and 1.57 mmol/h respectively. The same mass of catalyst was used in all reactions. Contact time was kept fixed across experiments. Reaction temperatures between 200ºC and 400ºC were examined. The target variable was the yield of oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid). Eleven descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis. Properties were calculated for isolated atoms using DFT-PBEsol and FHI-aims code. Per-element free-atom properties were converted to system-specific properties via composition-weighted average. Oxygen content was not included in the material's characterization. The quality function uses coverage and cumulative Jensen-Shannon divergence.

Procedures And Architectures
The subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence local approach was applied. SGD starts with the generation of a pool of propositions. Propositions are inequalities constraining the values of continuous candidate descriptive parameters. SGD identifies selectors formed by propositions and the AND connector. Selectors result in the selection of subgroups with outstanding target value distributions. The quality function measures how outstanding specific subselections of data points are. The coverage term controls the subgroup size and prevents small SGs. The Jensen-Shannon divergence measures dissimilarity between two distributions. The approach identifies a local behavior rather than a global model. For four-component materials, phosphorus content was fixed to 0.60. Ruthenium molar content was fixed to 0.05 for four-component materials. V_C elements were selected based on octahedral coordination and atomic radius difference. The maximum atomic radius difference compared to tungsten was 0.10 Å. Considered V_C elements included niobium, tantalum, chromium, molybdenum, tin, antimony, and tellurium. Lead was also included as it was experimentally tested.

Key Results
50% of the measured materials and conditions result in less than 2% oxygenates yield. Only 41 measurements out of 1220 are associated to yields of oxygenates above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set is equal to 4.83%. The maximum oxygenates yield value is 26.85%. The selected SG contains only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. The average yield of oxygenates in this SG is equal to 24.15%. The SG is described by rules: 280 ≤ T ≤ 300ºC, P > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. The highest yield of oxygenates for four-component materials is 60.19% at 400ºC. This highest yield contains 0.35 molar fraction of tellurium. The highest yield of oxygenates for five-component materials is 59.60% at 400ºC. This five-component catalyst contains tantalum as the V^ element. The composition-averaged electronegativity for this five-component material is 3.947 eV. The four- and five-component yields are up to twice as large as three-component materials. The SG for four- and five-component data contains 18 data points. The rules for the new SG constrain T ≥ 360ºC, L_+1 ≤ 1.001 Å, and VH < -1.593 eV.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The rules reflect the underlying processes particularly associated to high performance. High phosphorus content is needed to achieve outstanding performance. This could be related to the dilution of metal active sites. The electronegativity rule effectively limits the range of Ru contents. Ru is needed for conversion but too much leads to combustion products. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data used. The approach detects interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex patterns. The identified rules guide the design of more complex catalysts. The local modelling approach is suitable for search of exceptional materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
The atomic structures of all the tested catalysts are not known in detail. The oxygen content is not included in the material's characterization. The SG rule on reaction temperature is not transferable to four-component materials. It is unclear if the SG rules can identify exceptional materials for arbitrary Ru content. Different mechanisms may operate on materials with significantly different radii. The analysis was focused on low ruthenium contents. The SGD analysis might need new data points for unexplored portions of materials space.

Claims
SGD identifies specific physicochemical constraints that predict high catalytic performance in selective oxidation. The SG rules describe materials with outstanding catalytic performance. The rules constrain temperature, phosphorus content, and electronegativity. The temperature rule did not transfer to four-component materials. These rules can guide the design of new catalysts.
The derived rules successfully predict high-performing four- and five-component catalysts. Four-component catalysts achieved yields up to 60.19%. Five-component catalysts achieved yields up to 59.60%. The highest yields for complex materials occurred at higher temperatures. The approach generalizes to more complex materials.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and values for elemental properties are available in the ESI.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar SG rules are obtained when training with randomly-selected 90% of data points. Rules are similar when data points with yield lower than 3% are excluded. The ranges of variation for thresholds are similar to the main results. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the SGD approach and the selective oxidation reaction. Figure 2 shows the distribution of yield and the SG rules for three-component catalysts. Figure 3 shows the ternary diagram of Ru content. Figure 4 shows the catalyst map for four-component materials and experimental results. Figure 5 shows the SG analysis for four- and five-component materials.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the application of SGD to HTE and DFT data to find catalyst design rules. 2. The strongest evidence is the successful prediction of high-yield four- and five-component catalysts. 3. The future path involves exploring unexplored portions of the materials space.
